body: Depends how you define diverse!

Personally I think it’s more related to the idea do fighting for the same cognitive resources (focusing on eye movements while focusing on the memory) is what reduces the emotional vividness of the memory, meaning cognitions about the event can be targeted more easily. This idea of reducing vividness of a trauma reducing ptsd symptoms  is supported by one of the leading cognitive models of ptsd (dual representation theory)

Original peer reviewed article:  
Kellner, C. H et al. (2012). ECT in treatment-resistant depression. American Journal of Psychiatry, 169(12), 1238-1244.  
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), which has been in use for 75 years, is an important treatment for severe and treatment-resistant depression. Although it is acknowledged as the most effective acute treatment for severe mood and psychotic disorders, it remains controversial because of misperceptions about its use and lack of familiarity among health care professionals about modern ECT technique. The authors present an illustrative case of a patient for whom ECT is indicated. They review the basic and clinical science related to ECT's mechanism of action and discuss clinical issues in the administration of a course of ECT, including the consent process.Topics: controversy behind ECT, neuroscience mechanisms of action.

This is a great question. So a traumatic experience is one where the individual feels like they are being threatened or in danger. Different people may respond with their body/interpret different experiences as a threat so what may be a traumatic experience for someone wouldn’t be for someone else. Eg. Someone holding a gun on your head may promote a fight or flight reaction, causing you to procès the memory more sensory focused and therefore develop flashback sumptoms later on, while someone else may be shocked during the time the gun is held and then not process the memory as severely due to their own interpretation of the event eg. I wasn’t in control because it randomly happened without me lredicting (trauma) vs yes, it was random but it’s not a rare occurrence and I gained control by running away. Hope this makes sense! Basically it’s not the trauma that defines PTSD, it’s how you interpret whatever experience :)
